# VedicDateTime

**VedicDateTime** is an open-source R package that implements key components of the **Vedic calendar (lunisolar)** and provides conversions from **Gregorian date-time** (or **Julian Day Number**) to Vedic calendar entities.

The motivation is that many phenomena—especially in **time-series analysis**—can be influenced by both **solar** and **lunar** cycles. The package paper presents VedicDateTime and demonstrates two applied case studies using the package.

[Get started](getting-started.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}
[Reference](reference.qmd){.btn .btn-secondary}

:::

## What does the package compute?

VedicDateTime implements the core parts of **Panchanga** (“five arms” of the Vedic calendar):

- **Tithi** — lunar day (phase-based)
- **Vaara** — weekday
- **Nakshatra** — constellation segment based on the moon’s position
- **Yoga** — derived from sun + moon longitudes
- **Karana** — half-tithi

The package also includes additional related entities and utilities (see [Reference](reference.qmd)), such as:

- sunrise/sunset, moonrise/moonset
- solar/lunar longitudes
- rashi, lagna, masa, ritu, samvatsara
- Gregorian ↔ Julian day conversion helpers

## Why a lunisolar calendar?

Calendar systems can be **solar**, **lunar**, or **lunisolar**. The Gregorian calendar is a solar calendar and serves as a modern standard. However, Vedic calendars are lunisolar and can be useful when the analysis depends on the dynamics of both the sun and the moon.

The VedicDateTime paper motivates use in **calendar seasonality** and **moving-holiday effects** (e.g., festivals whose timing shifts under the Gregorian calendar).

## Quick example (from the paper)

Below is an example shown in the package paper (note: code is displayed; it is not executed when building this site).

```r
# Julian day number
jd <- 2459778

# Latitude, Longitude, and timezone of the location
place <- c(15.34, 75.13, +5.5)

tithi(jd, place)
#> [1] 20 20 55 35
```

Interpretation (as explained in the paper):

- The first number is the **tithi index** (there are 30 tithis).
- The remaining values indicate the **ending time** (hour, minute, second) for that tithi.

## Scope and outputs

Many functions return compact numeric vectors that include:

- an **index** (e.g., which tithi/nakshatra/yoga)
- the **end time** for the current entity (hour/minute/second)

In some situations, **two entities can occur on one date**, and the output may include both (e.g., two tithis with their end times). The paper also notes handling of skipped/leap cases.

## Citation

If you use VedicDateTime in academic work, please cite:

> Bokde, N. D., Patil, P. K., Sengupta, S., Sawant, M., & Feijóo-Lorenzo, A. E. (2023). *VedicDateTime: An R package to implement Vedic calendar system*. Multimedia Tools and Applications. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11042-023-16553-w
